query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition of a more ductile element, such as approximately 5 atomic percent titanium (Ti), into the equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy will improve room-temperature ductility by reducing the lattice’s Peierls barrier and enhancing dislocation mobility while retaining the high-temperature BCC phase stability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy with a single-phase BCC structure known for excellent high-temperature mechanical properties but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Partial substitution of approximately 5 at% of one constituent element with Ti to form a NbMoTaW–Ti alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under room temperature (for ductility evaluation), at 1600 °C (to assess high-temperature mechanical performance), and under irradiation conditions (to verify irradiation resistance).
generation.structural_mediator: The Ti addition is expected to modify local lattice distortions without triggering secondary phases; the slight change in atomic size and bonding can lower the activation barrier for dislocation motion, and the alloy remains a stable BCC solid solution.
generation.mechanism: Ti’s incorporation reduces the Peierls barrier by altering lattice distortions and enhancing dislocation mobility, thereby imparting improved plasticity at room temperature. Simultaneously, its limited content ensures that the high melting point and phase stability at elevated temperatures are preserved, and irradiation resistance is maintained due to the retained overall refractory matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated NbMoTaW alloy, the Ti-modified alloy will demonstrate increased ductility at room temperature (evidenced by higher elongation and lower yield strength) while exhibiting comparable high-temperature mechanical strength and unchanged irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy with no Ti addition.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is predicted when Ti is added in a precise, small quantity (~5 at%). Deviations from this concentration might lead to the formation of unwanted secondary phases or compromise high-temperature performance and irradiation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti content and its interaction with other elements in the NbMoTaW system are not fully established, and there is uncertainty over whether Ti may inadvertently affect other critical properties beyond ductility if not tightly controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of alloys: baseline NbMoTaW, NbMoTaW with 5 at% Ti substitution, and optionally a higher substitution level (e.g., 10 at% Ti). Process all samples identically using selective laser melting (SLM). Evaluate room-temperature tensile properties, high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical performance, and irradiation response through ion implantation tests.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile tests: yield strength, elongation to failure, and ductility measures.
High-temperature (1600 °C) compressive or tensile strength tests.
Irradiation damage assessment using ion implantation followed by microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, XRD).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 5 at% Ti alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., greater elongation or lower yield stress) without a measurable degradation of high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
## 1. Introduction
“Superalloy” is the general name given to iron-based, nickel-based, and cobalt-based alloys, given their high endurance, creep, and fatigue strength at high temperature.
